q: A 4-month-old unvaccinated puppy has had 2 days of haemorrhagic diarrhoea and vomiting. A faecal antigen ELISA (SNAP) test is negative. The most appropriate next step is to
o: isolate the puppy and submit faeces for quantitative PCR (qPCR).
release the puppy from isolation because a negative result excludes canine parvovirus (CPV).
manage as dietary indiscretion in the general ward and reassess in 48 hours.
e: Faecal antigen tests are highly specific but insensitive (false negatives reach about 51%), so a negative result does not exclude CPV in a compatible case. Isolate and confirm with qPCR. Releasing the puppy or moving it to the general ward exposes susceptible animals.

q: A healthy adult dog is given a modified live virus (MLV) DAPP vaccine at intake. Ten days later it is bright and eating, with normal faeces, but a faecal parvovirus qPCR is positive. The most likely explanation is
o: subclinical canine parvovirus (CPV) infection acquired from the shelter environment.
shedding of vaccine-derived virus.
cross-reactivity of the assay with canine coronavirus.
e: Up to about 23% of recently MLV-vaccinated dogs are qPCR-positive between days 3 and 28. In a clinically normal dog this is interpreted cautiously and does not by itself indicate field infection. Because qPCR targets parvovirus nucleic acid, cross-reaction with coronavirus is not the usual explanation.

q: Which finding within the first 24 hours of hospitalisation is the most reliable positive predictor of survival in a puppy with canine parvovirus (CPV) enteritis?
o: Resolution of vomiting after the first antiemetic dose
Normalisation of the packed cell volume by 24 hours
A measurable rise in the absolute lymphocyte count
e: An early lymphocyte rebound carries a 100% positive predictive value for survival. Vomiting can settle transiently and does not predict outcome, and the packed cell volume is driven by fluid status and gut blood loss rather than by recovery of the marrow.

q: After fluid resuscitation, a puppy with canine parvovirus (CPV) enteritis has fever, hypoglycaemia and signs of sepsis. Which antimicrobial combination is best supported for this puppy?
o: Cefovecin plus metronidazole
Ampicillin plus amikacin
Enrofloxacin plus metronidazole
e: Up to 72% of Gram-negative isolates from CPV sepsis resist third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins and metronidazole, so an ampicillin-plus-aminoglycoside backbone is preferred once the puppy is rehydrated (limiting nephrotoxicity). Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in growing puppies.

q: A 12-week-old puppy with parvoviral enteritis is 8% dehydrated, has a body condition score (BCS) of 5/9 and is bright and responsive. The shelter has no space in its isolation ward. Which plan is best supported?
o: Subcutaneous fluids and oral care from admission, with IV fluids only if vomiting worsens
IV fluids for 24 hours, then step down to subcutaneous fluids and oral care in foster
Humane euthanasia, because treatment cannot be delivered safely without an isolation ward
e: A hybrid model corrects dehydration, hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia with IV fluids in the first 24 hours before stepping down; outpatient survival is about 80 to 83%. Euthanasia thresholds are BCS under 3/9, recumbency or non-responsiveness, none of which this puppy has.

q: A kennel that housed a puppy with canine parvovirus (CPV) has had organic debris removed. Which disinfection regimen is effective for the cleaned surface?
o: Accelerated hydrogen peroxide 1:32 with 10 minutes of contact time
Quaternary ammonium compound at label dilution with 10 minutes of contact time
70% alcohol spray with 1 minute of contact time
e: CPV is a non-enveloped virus. Accelerated hydrogen peroxide (1:32, 10 min), bleach (1:32, 10 min) and 1% potassium peroxymonosulfate (10 min) are effective. Quaternary ammonium compounds and alcohol are unreliable against non-enveloped viruses.

q: During a canine parvovirus (CPV) outbreak, a well 7-month-old dog with no vaccination history shared a run with an affected puppy 3 days ago. What is the most appropriate way to categorise and manage this dog?
o: High risk; quarantine for 14 days regardless of any test result
Low risk; continue normal adoption without testing because the dog is over 5 months old
Moderate risk; perform antibody titre testing and reclassify if the titre is adequate
e: Dogs over 5 months with no vaccination history and possible exposure are moderate risk. Titre testing lets protected dogs be reclassified as low risk and placed. Puppies under 5 months are the group that is high risk regardless of history.

q: An asymptomatic dog received a modified live virus (MLV) distemper vaccine 5 days ago. A nasal swab reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) for canine distemper virus (CDV) is positive with a very low cycle threshold (Ct). The most appropriate interpretation is
o: probable wild-type infection, because a low Ct indicates a high viral load.
vaccine virus shedding, because recent MLV vaccination always produces a positive result.
an uninterpretable result that should be repeated after 6 weeks.
e: Vaccine virus produces only a low viral load (high Ct). A low Ct (high load) is highly suggestive of active field infection, and a dog with a strongly positive result should be managed as infected.

q: Which histologic finding best supports a diagnosis of canine distemper in a dog with neurological signs?
o: Basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies in hepatocytes and vascular endothelium
Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic Negri bodies in hippocampal neurons
Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic and intranuclear inclusions in astrocytes and epithelial cells
e: Canine distemper produces both intracytoplasmic and intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions. Intranuclear basophilic inclusions in liver and endothelium suggest canine adenovirus-1, and Negri bodies suggest rabies.

q: A 9-month-old shelter dog recovered from a mild fever and cough 3 weeks ago. It now has myoclonus and progressive ataxia. The most likely cause is
o: canine distemper virus neurological disease after resolution of systemic signs.
delayed neurological spread of canine adenovirus-2 infection.
Neospora caninum protozoal encephalitis.
e: Canine distemper is biphasic and neurological signs can appear 1 to 3 weeks or longer after systemic signs resolve, carrying a poor prognosis. Canine adenovirus-2 causes respiratory rather than neurological disease. Neospora is a differential for neurological signs but the history fits distemper.

q: Which statement about shedding of canine distemper virus (CDV) after recovery is correct?
o: There is no true carrier state, but shedding may persist for up to 16 weeks.
Recovered dogs become lifelong carriers that intermittently shed the virus.
Shedding stops within 48 hours of resolution of clinical signs.
e: CDV has no true carrier state, yet shedding can continue for up to 16 weeks and some dogs remain low-level PCR-positive for months, so they are kept away from susceptible dogs.

q: In a shelter, several 17-week-old puppies from dams that recovered from field canine distemper virus (CDV) infection fail to respond to modified live virus (MLV) vaccination. The most likely explanation is
o: persistent high maternal antibody blocking vaccine virus beyond the usual 16 weeks.
a vaccine strain from a different serotype than the field strain.
vaccine-induced immunosuppression from a concurrent parvovirus vaccine.
e: Very high maternal antibody from dams that recovered from field infection can block MLV past 16 weeks, so shelter series are extended to 20 weeks. CDV has one serotype, so serotype mismatch does not explain vaccine failure.

q: Canine adenovirus-2 differs from canine respiratory coronavirus and canine influenza virus in that it is
o: enveloped, and therefore inactivated by quaternary ammonium.
non-enveloped, and therefore reliably inactivated by alcohol-based sanitisers.
non-enveloped, and therefore resistant to alcohol-based sanitisers and quaternary ammonium.
e: Canine adenovirus-2 is the only non-enveloped (DNA) virus among the main respiratory pathogens; it is environmentally stable and resists alcohol and quaternary ammonium. Enveloped agents are susceptible to both.

q: A shelter dog has fever, lethargy, anorexia and a productive cough. A complete blood count shows leukocytosis with a left shift. These findings are most consistent with
o: uncomplicated viral upper respiratory infection.
bacterial pneumonia complicating respiratory disease.
a stress leukogram from kennel confinement.
e: Uncomplicated respiratory disease usually leaves the dog bright and eating with a stress leukogram. Anorexia, fever and an inflammatory leukogram with a left shift indicate lower airway bacterial disease.

q: A technician accidentally injects an intranasal Bordetella bronchiseptica vaccine subcutaneously. Which outcome should be anticipated?
o: Cellulitis or abscess at the injection site, with a risk of hepatocellular necrosis
Transient local swelling only, because the vaccine organism is non-viable
Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia within 7 days of injection
e: Live intranasal Bordetella vaccine given SQ is a significant error: it can cause cellulitis, abscessation and acute hepatocellular necrosis with liver failure, and is treated with doxycycline. The vaccine organism is live.

q: Several dogs in a kennel die suddenly with haemorrhagic pneumonia within 48 hours of the onset of coughing, and Streptococcus zooepidemicus is cultured. Which antimicrobial is appropriate for the exposed dogs?
o: Doxycycline 5 mg/kg PO every 12 hours
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg PO once daily
A beta-lactam such as penicillin G or cefovecin
e: Streptococcus zooepidemicus is resistant to doxycycline and requires a beta-lactam, given prophylactically to exposed dogs because disease is rapid and deadly. Macrolides are reserved for culture-confirmed resistant lower-airway disease.

q: A human influenza A antigen kit is used on a nasal swab from a coughing dog and the result is negative. Which statement is correct?
o: The dog can be released from quarantine because the negative result is reliable.
The result is uninformative because these kits have poor sensitivity in dogs.
A positive result would be unreliable, but a negative result reliably excludes canine influenza.
e: Human antigen kits have poor canine sensitivity. A positive is reliable but a negative cannot clear an animal. Confirmation requires PCR.

q: Compared with H3N8, isolation of a dog with H3N2 canine influenza virus is longer because
o: H3N2 is spread only by direct contact, so a fixed 14 days is required.
shedding is prolonged and intermittent, so about 21 to 28 days is needed.
H3N2 produces a persistent lifelong carrier state in recovered dogs.
e: H3N8 isolation is about 7 to 10 days; H3N2 is about 21 to 28 days because of prolonged intermittent shedding. Neither subtype produces a true carrier state and both spread by aerosol, droplets, contact and fomites.

q: During an active canine influenza virus outbreak, the manager proposes vaccinating every dog to stop the spread. The best response is
o: to agree, because one dose of the vaccine gives protection within 48 hours.
to decline, because the killed vaccine needs two doses 2 to 3 weeks apart before protection.
to decline, because the vaccine is contraindicated in dogs already exposed.
e: The two-dose killed vaccine with delayed protection cannot stop an outbreak already underway; it is also non-core and does not prevent infection. Control depends on isolation, cohorting and sanitation.

q: A stray kitten with patchy alopecia and scaling is examined with a Wood's lamp and no fluorescence is seen. This finding
o: rules out dermatophytosis, so no culture is required.
excludes Microsporum canis, although Trichophyton remains possible.
does not rule out dermatophytosis, because many infected cats do not fluoresce.
e: Only M. canis fluoresces apple-green, and only in about half of cases. A positive is strongly indicative, but a negative never rules out ringworm.

q: A lesion-free cat that is Wood's lamp negative has a dermatophyte test medium (DTM) culture growing Microsporum canis at 2 colony-forming units (CFU). The most appropriate classification and plan is
o: an infected cat: begin systemic itraconazole and keep isolated until cured.
a contaminant: disregard the result because M. canis is normal feline flora.
a fomite (dust-mop) carrier: re-culture, give one lime sulfur dip and proceed to adoption.
e: This is a P1 result in a lesion-free cat, consistent with mechanical carriage. Microsporum canis is never normal flora, so every positive needs action, but this action is proportionate (dip-and-go), not full treatment.

q: By day 5, a toothbrush culture plate from a crusted stray cat is fully red and covered in heavy, dark, pigmented, fuzzy colonies. This finding is most consistent with
o: Trichophyton infection; begin treatment immediately.
Microsporum canis infection; begin treatment immediately.
saprophytic contamination; record as heavy contamination and reculture.
e: Dermatophytes are typically pale and turn the medium red as they grow. Heavy pigmented overgrowth is saprophytic contamination that can mask true positives, so it is recorded as heavy contamination and re-cultured.

q: Which is the preferred systemic antifungal regimen for a shelter cat with ringworm?
o: Griseofulvin 25 mg/kg PO twice daily for 6 to 8 weeks, plus lime sulfur
Ketoconazole 10 mg/kg PO once daily for 4 weeks, plus lime sulfur
Itraconazole 5 to 10 mg/kg PO once daily for 21 to 28 days, plus lime sulfur
e: Itraconazole is preferred. Griseofulvin is avoided (long cure time, teratogenicity, and idiosyncratic irreversible marrow suppression that is potentially lethal in FeLV- or FIV-positive cats). Ketoconazole is poorly tolerated in cats and not a shelter first choice.

q: After hair and debris are mechanically removed from a cat room, which disinfectant is effective against ringworm spores?
o: 1% potassium peroxymonosulfate
Quaternary ammonium at label dilution
2% potassium peroxymonosulfate
e: Ringworm needs a 2% potassium peroxymonosulfate solution; 1% is unreliable against spores (unlike parvovirus, where 1% works). Quaternary ammonium compounds are ineffective for both.

q: Three cats in one room are being treated for ringworm. Two have had three consecutive negative weekly cultures and the third is still positive. Which is correct?
o: Release the two negative cats after a final lime sulfur dip.
Release the two negative cats to foster with a repeat culture in 2 weeks.
Hold all three until the third cat also reaches mycological cure.
e: Co-housed animals are released only when every animal in the group is cured, because a negative cat sharing space with a positive one is re-contaminated.

q: A litter of 5-week-old kittens has a wide-based stance, hypermetria and intention tremor, with normal mentation. The signs have not progressed. The queen was unvaccinated and had panleukopenia in mid-gestation. The most likely cause of the kittens' signs is
o: congenital hydrocephalus from obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow.
cerebellar hypoplasia from perinatal infection of the cerebellum.
Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis acquired from the queen.
e: In-utero or perinatal feline panleukopenia virus infection produces non-progressive cerebellar hypoplasia with normal mentation. Progressive signs or altered mentation would point toward hydrocephalus or encephalitis.

q: An FIV-positive adult cat in a shelter requires protection against feline panleukopenia. Which product is appropriate?
o: A modified live virus (MLV) FVRCP vaccine, as for other cats
No vaccination, because FIV-positive cats cannot respond to any vaccine
An inactivated feline panleukopenia vaccine
e: Modified live virus vaccine can precipitate vaccine-induced panleukopenia in immunocompromised cats, so FIV-positive cats receive an inactivated product.

q: During a feline panleukopenia outbreak, which statement about antibody titre testing to triage exposed cats is correct?
o: A canine parvovirus antibody kit is a valid substitute, because both viruses share one serotype.
A feline-specific assay is required, because canine kits do not reliably detect feline antibody.
Titre testing is unreliable in cats and should not be used to triage exposed cats.
e: Canine kits cannot reliably detect FPV antibody in cats. A validated feline-specific assay (haemagglutination inhibition titre of 80 or higher is protective) is used.

q: A 4-month-old kitten from a stray litter tests positive for feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) antibody on a point-of-care test. These results indicate
o: persistent FIV infection; manage as FIV-positive from now on.
probable maternal antibody; retest at 5 to 6 months of age.
prior FIV vaccination; retest with a PCR assay only.
e: Under 6 months a positive antibody test is almost always maternal antibody (vertical FIV transmission is rare). Retest until 5 to 6 months before calling the kitten infected. FIV vaccination is not recommended in shelters.

q: An adult cat is negative for FeLV p27 antigen on whole blood and negative on immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) testing, but quantitative PCR detects a low proviral copy number. This pattern most likely reflects
o: abortive infection.
regressive infection.
progressive infection.
e: Regressive infection features latent provirus in marrow, a negative IFA and a low proviral load. Abortive infection is negative on antigen, IFA and PCR. Progressive infection is generally positive on all three, with a high copy number.

q: A cat is bitten by an FIV-positive cat and shares food dishes with an FeLV-positive cat. Point-of-care tests 10 days later are negative for both. What retest interval is recommended?
o: Both viruses at 14 days after exposure
FeLV at 60 days and FIV at 30 days after exposure
FeLV at 30 days and FIV at 60 days after exposure
e: FeLV p27 antigenaemia can take up to 30 days to appear and FIV antibody up to 60 days. Testing earlier can produce false negatives.

q: A healthy unweaned 3-week-old kitten from a stray litter tests positive for FeLV antigen on whole blood at intake. The best management is to
o: euthanise the kitten to prevent transmission.
isolate the kitten from unrelated litters and retest at adoption age.
place the kitten in foster with unrelated kittens as an FeLV-positive cat.
e: Many antigen-positive neonates revert as early transient antigenaemia becomes regressive infection, typically within about 16 weeks. A healthy unweaned kitten should not be euthanised on a single intake result, but it should be kept away from unrelated litters.

q: A 2-year-old cat presents with dyspnoea. Radiographs show a cranial mediastinal mass with pleural effusion, and cytology is consistent with T-cell lymphoma. Which underlying infection is most likely?
o: FeLV infection
FIV infection
Feline coronavirus infection
e: FeLV classically drives mediastinal (thymic) T-cell lymphoma in young cats. FIV is more associated with B-cell lymphoma (gastrointestinal or nasal) in older cats.

q: A trap-neuter-return programme manager asks whether all trapped community cats should be tested for FeLV and FIV before return. Which advice is best supported?
o: Test all cats and euthanise positives, because returning infected cats endangers the colony.
Routine testing is not recommended; seroprevalence resembles owned cats and sterilisation reduces transmission.
Test only cats over 6 months of age and vaccinate FeLV-negative cats before return.
e: Positive cats add no extra threat if they remain outdoors, and resources are better spent on sterilisation, which removes nursing (FeLV) and fight-bite (both) transmission.

q: A 10-month-old cat has a straw-yellow, viscous abdominal effusion with high protein and an albumin:globulin ratio of 0.4. A standard feline coronavirus RT-PCR on the effusion is positive. This result
o: confirms coronavirus but does not distinguish FIP from enteric coronavirus infection.
confirms FIP, because coronavirus in an effusion is diagnostic of the disease.
is a false positive from faecal contamination and should be disregarded.
e: Enteric coronavirus can circulate in monocytes and reach extra-intestinal sites, so a positive standard PCR confirms exposure, not mutation to FIPV. The definitive test is antigen within macrophages in pyogranulomatous lesions.

q: Which statement about the Rivalta test on an effusion from a cat suspected of FIP is correct?
o: It is highly specific but poorly sensitive, so a positive result confirms FIP while a negative does not exclude it.
It is highly sensitive but poorly specific, so a negative is reassuring while positives occur in other effusions.
It has low sensitivity and low specificity, so neither a positive nor a negative result should influence the diagnosis.
e: Reported Rivalta sensitivity is about 91 to 98% but specificity only about 66 to 80%. A negative lowers suspicion; a positive does not confirm FIP.

q: A shelter cat has fever, ulcers on the tongue and hard palate, and lameness that resolves within 48 hours. The most likely pathogen is
o: feline calicivirus.
feline herpesvirus-1.
Chlamydia felis.
e: Oral and tongue ulcers and febrile limping syndrome are characteristic of calicivirus. Herpesvirus is associated with dendritic corneal ulcers, and Chlamydia felis with chemosis and conjunctivitis.

q: Several vaccinated cats in one room die within a week, with oedema of the head and paws and cutaneous ulceration, and the disease spreads quickly within the enclosure. The most likely diagnosis is
o: feline herpesvirus-1 recrudescence.
virulent systemic feline calicivirus.
feline panleukopenia virus infection.
e: Virulent systemic calicivirus is suspected with high mortality, severe vasculitis with head and paw oedema, and rapid spread; the routine calicivirus vaccine does not reliably protect. Herpesvirus recrudescence does not cause this systemic vasculitis.

q: A shelter cat with acute upper respiratory disease is suspected of Mycoplasma felis and Chlamydia felis infection. Which is the best first-line antibiotic?
o: Amoxicillin, given twice daily with food
Doxycycline, given as a liquid followed by water or food
Cefovecin, given as a single injection
e: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so beta-lactams (amoxicillin, cefovecin) that target peptidoglycan are ineffective; amoxicillin is acceptable only when Mycoplasma and Chlamydia are not suspected. Doxycycline tablets can cause oesophageal strictures, so liquid with a water or food flush is used.

q: A cat vaccinated with an intranasal modified live virus FVRCP vaccine 5 days ago is sneezing. A PCR panel is positive for feline herpesvirus-1 and Mycoplasma felis. The best interpretation is that
o: both results confirm primary disease from each organism separately.
the herpesvirus result indicates vaccine failure, so revaccination is required.
the herpesvirus result may reflect vaccine shedding, and Mycoplasma is not proven causal.
e: Intranasal MLV vaccination can cause false-positive herpesvirus and calicivirus PCR results for 1 to 3 weeks, and Mycoplasma is frequently part of normal flora, so PCR does not prove causation.

q: A shelter manager proposes 14-day quarantine for all healthy incoming cats to reduce upper respiratory disease. The best response is
o: to agree, because quarantine before general housing lowers respiratory disease risk.
to decline, because a longer stay is the greatest risk factor; vaccinate at intake instead.
to modify the plan so that only kittens under 4 months of age are quarantined.
e: Length of stay is the single greatest URTD risk factor, so routine quarantine of healthy unexposed cats is avoided in favour of intake vaccination, good housing and low length of stay.

q: A dog imported from Mexico has a history of late-term abortion. A rapid slide agglutination test for Brucella canis in the clinic is positive. The most appropriate next step is to
o: isolate the dog and confirm with agar gel immunodiffusion, culture or PCR.
euthanise the dog immediately, because a positive result confirms infection.
spay the dog and begin doxycycline and rifampin without further testing.
e: The rapid slide agglutination test has a high false-positive rate, so isolation is required but disposition decisions need confirmation. B. canis is zoonotic and not reliably cleared by treatment, so confirmation matters before any treatment or euthanasia decision.

q: A 3-year-old FIV-positive cat has severe lethargy, pale mucous membranes, a packed cell volume of 12% and PCR-confirmed Mycoplasma haemofelis infection. Which management is most appropriate?
o: Doxycycline 10 mg/kg PO once daily for 28 days, with prednisolone if immune-mediated and transfusion if packed cell volume is under 15%
Ronidazole 30 mg/kg PO once daily for 14 days, adding prednisolone and transfusing only if the cat becomes recumbent
Amoxicillin-clavulanate PO for 14 days, with prednisolone started at diagnosis and transfusion only if the cat collapses
e: Doxycycline is first-line for haemoplasmosis (once daily in cats to reduce oesophageal stricture risk), with prednisolone for an immune-mediated component and transfusion for severe anaemia. Ronidazole is used for Tritrichomonas foetus, and amoxicillin is not effective against a wall-less organism.

q: A cluster of kittens has persistent watery diarrhoea and Cryptosporidium oocysts are identified. Which decontamination method is required for the housing?
o: Steam at 140°F (60°C) or above, or 6% hydrogen peroxide for 30 minutes
Bleach diluted 1:32 with 10 minutes of contact time
Quaternary ammonium compound at label dilution for 10 minutes
e: Cryptosporidium oocysts resist chlorine disinfectants including standard bleach dilutions. Steam (140°F / 60°C or above) or 6% hydrogen peroxide (30 min) is required, making it one of the hardest pathogens to decontaminate in a shelter.

q: A puppy was exposed to a parvovirus-shedding littermate 3 days ago and is still bright and eating. Which statement about viral shedding is correct?
o: Shedding begins only once diarrhoea is first noticed and stops when it resolves.
Shedding usually begins about 4 to 7 days after infection and can precede clinical signs.
Shedding begins about 14 to 21 days after infection, so a puppy at day 3 is safe to move.
e: Incubation of canine parvovirus is 4 to 14 days, and shedding starts around day 4 to 7, often before signs appear. This is why exposed-but-healthy animals must be managed as potentially infectious.

q: Why is the subclinical form of canine parvovirus especially dangerous in a shelter?
o: Affected animals shed a virus that is more resistant to disinfectants.
Affected animals look healthy but still shed virus.
Affected animals transmit the virus only by the airborne route.
e: Subclinical puppies (with maternal antibody) or low-titre adults shed virus while looking well, driving silent transmission.

q: The myocardial form of canine parvovirus has become rare mainly because
o: breeding bitches are vaccinated, protecting neonates.
modern vaccines contain a myocardial-specific antigen.
puppies are now usually weaned before 4 weeks of age.
e: Myocardial disease follows in-utero or very early infection, and maternal vaccination and maternal antibody have made it rare.

q: Canine parvovirus causes its intestinal lesions primarily by destroying
o: the crypt germinal epithelium, preventing villous renewal.
the villous tip enterocytes only, leaving the crypts intact.
the submucosal ganglia, causing paralytic ileus.
e: Crypt germinal epithelium destruction halts villous renewal, causing villous atrophy, malabsorption, and barrier loss with bacterial translocation. Rapidly dividing cells are the targets.

q: Which canine parvovirus variant can produce severe panleukopenia-like disease in cats?
o: The original CPV-2
CPV-1 (minute virus of canines)
CPV-2c
e: CPV-2a, 2b and 2c can infect cats, and 2c can cause severe panleukopenia-like disease. The original CPV-2 did not infect cats.

q: Which finding is a recognised poor prognostic indicator in a puppy with canine parvovirus?
o: A rising absolute lymphocyte count
Marked, persistent leukopenia
A serum albumin above the reference range
e: Poor prognosis is associated with marked persistent leukopenia, severe hypoalbuminaemia, low haematocrit, hypoglycaemia and persistently elevated 72-hour cortisol.

q: Maropitant should be used with caution in which patient group?
o: Puppies over 12 weeks of age, because of a hepatotoxicity risk
Puppies under 8 weeks of age, because of a bone-marrow hypoplasia risk
Adult dogs with hypoalbuminaemia, because of a risk of protein-losing enteropathy
e: Maropitant carries a bone-marrow hypoplasia caution in puppies under 8 weeks of age.

q: Which statement about nutrition in canine parvovirus enteritis is best supported?
o: Food should be withheld until vomiting has stopped for at least 48 hours.
Parenteral nutrition is required in all puppies to protect the gut.
Early enteral nutrition before vomiting has fully resolved improves outcomes.
e: Early enteral feeding, starting at about 25% of resting energy requirement and building to 100% by day 2 to 4, shortens recovery.

q: Which adjunctive therapy for canine parvovirus has randomised evidence of no significant survival benefit?
o: Early enteral nutrition
Immune or hyperimmune plasma
Balanced isotonic crystalloid resuscitation
e: Randomised data show immune plasma gives no significant survival or clinical benefit. Hyperimmune plasma lowered 24-hour shock index and lactate but did not change survival.

q: How is a hypovolaemic puppy with canine parvovirus enteritis resuscitated with crystalloid?
o: A single 60 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes, followed by maintenance fluids only
Boluses of 15 to 20 mL/kg over about 15 minutes, repeated to a total of about 80 to 90 mL/kg
A slow infusion of 5 mL/kg per hour for the first 24 hours
e: Give 15 to 20 mL/kg boluses over about 15 minutes, repeated to a total of about 80 to 90 mL/kg, until perfusion is restored.

q: A resource-limited shelter is weighing euthanasia for canine parvovirus patients. Which finding meets the cited welfare threshold?
o: A body condition score of 5/9, 6% dehydration and a bright demeanour
A body condition score under 3/9, recumbency and non-responsiveness
A body condition score of 4/9, vomiting but still eating small meals
e: Cited thresholds for considering euthanasia are body condition score under 3/9, recumbency or non-responsiveness, plus inability to isolate or treat safely.

q: A shelter places a footbath at the door of its parvovirus ward. Which statement is correct?
o: Footbaths are effective if the disinfectant is a quaternary ammonium compound.
Footbaths are not an effective control strategy; dedicated footwear and barrier flooring are used instead.
Footbaths are effective if staff step through them for at least 30 seconds.
e: Footbaths are unreliable (organic matter accumulates and contact time is inadequate) and can spread pathogens.

q: Bedding and toys from a puppy with parvovirus are heavily contaminated. What is the recommended approach?
o: Wash them with other laundry on a hot cycle, because heat destroys parvovirus.
Air dry them for 24 hours and return them to general use.
Dispose of heavily contaminated soft items, since communal washing can spread the virus.
e: Communal washing can spread virus, so disposal of heavily contaminated soft items is frequently more practical. Spot cleaning a cage is acceptable when it is not visibly soiled.

q: What outcomes are expected for canine parvovirus with and without treatment?
o: Untreated mortality is about 40%, and treated survival is typically 60 to 70%.
Untreated mortality is below 10%, and treated survival is over 98%.
Untreated mortality can reach about 91%, and treated survival is typically 80 to 90%.
e: Untreated mortality can reach around 91%, and treated survival is generally 80 to 90%, with the first 3 to 5 days the most critical.

q: A puppy has recovered clinically from parvovirus and a faecal antigen ELISA is now negative. Which test is more reliable for confirming that shedding has stopped?
o: A repeat faecal antigen ELISA in 1 week
A complete blood count showing recovery of the leukocyte count
Faecal qPCR
e: Dogs can shed detectable viral DNA after signs resolve and the ELISA turns negative. If qPCR is unavailable, isolate for at least 2 weeks after recovery and bathe before release.

q: Which statement about the transmission and persistence of canine parvovirus is correct?
o: Spread is faecal-oral with heavy fomite transmission, and the virus can persist in the environment for over a year.
Spread is by aerosol, and the virus is inactivated within a few hours at room temperature.
Spread is by direct contact only, and the virus survives on surfaces for about 24 hours.
e: Faecal-oral and oronasal spread predominate, with heavy fomite transmission because the virus is environmentally stable. It can persist for over a year in cool, shaded, organic-rich conditions.

q: Vaccines developed in the 1950s and 1960s are still effective against canine distemper virus because
o: the virus mutates slowly and vaccine strains are updated every few years.
the virus has a single serotype, so outbreaks reflect coverage gaps, not antigenic escape.
cross-protective antibody is provided by the canine parvovirus vaccine.
e: Only one CDV serotype exists, so cross-protective MLV vaccines remain effective.

q: What is the earliest immunologic effect of canine distemper virus infection?
o: A marked neutrophilia with a left shift
Severe T and B lymphocytopenia with immunosuppression
A transient rise in eosinophil count
e: Early infection causes marked T and B lymphocytopenia and immunosuppression that can last for weeks.

q: Which statement about the transmission and environmental stability of canine distemper virus is correct?
o: It spreads by the faecal-oral route, and it persists in soil for over a year.
It spreads by fleas and ticks, and it survives well on dry surfaces in warm conditions.
It spreads by direct contact and aerosol, and it is labile, surviving minutes to a few hours when warm.
e: Direct contact and droplet or aerosol inhalation dominate. As an enveloped virus it is labile, with short survival at warm temperatures, but it persists 9 to 11 days at 39°F (4°C).

q: What is the frequently missed earliest sign of canine distemper?
o: Nasal hyperkeratosis
Pyrexia
Myoclonus
e: Early pyrexia within days to a week is commonly missed, especially in shelters.

q: Which examination is recommended in every dog with suspected canine distemper, and what dermatological sign may be seen?
o: A careful ocular examination; digital and nasal hyperkeratosis (hard pad)
A neurological examination only; generalised alopecia
An abdominal ultrasound; cutaneous ulceration of the ear tips
e: Ocular signs are common (discharge, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, retinal lesions, optic neuritis), so an ocular examination is indicated in all suspects. Hard pad is often linked to neurological disease.

q: Which statement about treatment of canine distemper is correct?
o: There is no antiviral; care is supportive, and neurological disease responds less well than other signs.
Ribavirin is effective if started within 48 hours of the first clinical signs.
Neurological signs respond best to treatment and usually resolve completely.
e: No antiviral exists. Care is supportive, with broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics and B vitamins for GI signs, and neurological disease is often progressive and irreversible.

q: What is the single most important measure to prevent canine distemper in shelters, and which vaccine type is preferred?
o: Quarantining all incoming dogs for 14 days, using a killed vaccine
Vaccinating all dogs at or before intake, using a modified live vaccine
Testing all incoming dogs by PCR, using a recombinant vaccine only
e: Intake vaccination is the most important control measure. MLV is preferred because it is cheaper and can protect before humoral immunity develops.

q: An exposed, asymptomatic adult dog has a positive canine distemper antibody titre and a negative RT-PCR. How should it be categorised?
o: Moderate risk, so it is quarantined for 14 days before adoption
High risk, so it is isolated with the affected dogs
Low risk and protected, so it is cleared for adoption or transfer
e: A positive titre with a negative PCR means the dog is immune and not shedding, so it is low risk and can be adopted or transferred.

q: An exposed, asymptomatic dog has a negative canine distemper antibody titre and a negative RT-PCR. How should this dog be managed?
o: It is protected, so it can be moved directly to the adoption floor.
It is susceptible, so vaccinate and quarantine it away from the outbreak footprint.
It is infected, so it should be isolated with the clinical cases.
e: A negative titre plus a negative PCR means no current infection but no immunity. The dog is susceptible, so it is vaccinated and quarantined separately.

q: Which set of measures describes a clean break during a canine distemper outbreak?
o: Vaccinate only dogs that show clinical signs, and keep all dogs in the same ward with separate cages
Move exposed dogs to the adoption floor after 7 days and admit new dogs to the intake ward
Vaccinate every incoming dog at entry, house dogs about 25 ft (7.6 m) or more from exposed dogs, and use separate staff and supplies
e: A clean break means vaccinating every incoming dog at entry, housing them about 25 ft (7.6 m) (ideally in a separate ward or building) from exposed dogs, with separate staff and supplies.

q: A recently MLV-vaccinated dog tests RT-PCR positive for canine distemper virus. Which vaccine is not detected by this assay?
o: The modified live CDV vaccine
Any vaccine combined with a parvovirus component
The canarypox-vectored recombinant CDV vaccine
e: MLV CDV replicates in the same cells as wild virus and can be PCR positive for about 2 weeks. The canarypox recombinant does not replicate, so it is not detected.

q: Canine infectious respiratory disease (CIRD) is best described as
o: a multifactorial complex involving host, agent and environment.
a single-pathogen disease caused by Bordetella bronchiseptica.
a viral disease caused only by canine influenza virus.
e: CIRD is multifactorial: multiple pathogens plus host and environmental stressors drive disease.

q: Which pairing of agent and mechanism in canine respiratory disease is correct?
o: Canine respiratory coronavirus infects the lower airway only, and Mycoplasma cynos has a cell wall.
Canine respiratory coronavirus denudes respiratory cilia, and Mycoplasma cynos uses sialidase to adhere to epithelium.
Canine respiratory coronavirus is a DNA virus, and Mycoplasma cynos is spread by fleas.
e: Canine respiratory coronavirus is nicknamed the lawnmower virus because it denudes respiratory cilia. Mycoplasma cynos, a wall-less bacterium, uses sialidase to adhere to and damage respiratory epithelium.

q: Which statement about the transmission of canine respiratory pathogens and their zoonotic risk is correct?
o: They spread only by direct contact, and no respiratory pathogen in dogs is zoonotic.
They spread by droplets up to about 6 m (20 ft) and by fomites, and Bordetella and Streptococcus zooepidemicus are zoonotic.
They spread by droplets up to 30 cm (1 ft), and only canine influenza virus is zoonotic.
e: Spread is largely by respiratory droplets, which travel up to about 6 m (20 ft), plus fomites. Bordetella and Streptococcus zooepidemicus are zoonotic, so staff wear protective clothing, gloves and eye or face protection.

q: Which dogs give the highest-yield samples for canine respiratory PCR during an outbreak?
o: Recovered dogs sampled 2 weeks after signs resolved
Healthy dogs sampled on the day of intake
Acutely ill dogs sampled within 1 to 2 days of onset
e: Sample acutely ill dogs within 1 to 2 days. After 5 to 7 days the shedding window closes and PCR loses value, so paired serology is used instead.

q: Which cleaning method is preferred in wards with canine respiratory disease?
o: High-pressure sprayers, to remove debris from kennel walls
Methods that limit aerosolisation, such as hose-end foamers
Steam jets aimed at the ceiling to humidify and sanitise the air
e: Cleaning should limit aerosolisation, so hose-end foamers are used rather than pressure sprayers. Aerosolisation and humidity spread pathogens.

q: Which statement about vaccines for canine respiratory disease is correct?
o: Only the distemper vaccine induces sterilising immunity, and intranasal vaccination is generally superior for respiratory agents except adenovirus-2.
All core respiratory vaccines induce sterilising immunity, and the parenteral route is superior for every agent.
Only the Bordetella vaccine induces sterilising immunity, and oral vaccination is the most effective route.
e: Only the CDV vaccine gives sterilising immunity. Intranasal mucosal vaccination is generally superior, with adenovirus-2 the exception, for which parenteral vaccination gives 4 or more years of immunity.

q: How many air changes per hour are recommended in shelter housing, and how should isolation be zoned?
o: About 2 to 4, with air recirculated between isolation and the general population
About 30 to 40, with a shared HVAC zone for all dog housing
About 10 to 12, ideally 100% outdoor air, with separately zoned HVAC for isolation
e: Aim for 10 to 12 air changes per hour, ideally 100% outdoor air, with separately zoned HVAC for isolation.

q: Which statement about quarantine and isolation in canine respiratory disease is correct?
o: All incoming dogs are quarantined for 14 days, and an improving case is isolated for 30 days.
Healthy unexposed dogs are quarantined for 7 days, and an improving case is released as soon as coughing stops.
Healthy unexposed dogs are not routinely quarantined, and an improving uncomplicated case is isolated for about 7 to 10 days.
e: Routine quarantine of healthy unexposed dogs is avoided, because prolonged length of stay is itself the greatest CIRD risk factor. Most improving cases are released at 7 to 10 days, weighing resolution of signs, shedding and housing risk.

q: When are antitussives appropriate in canine respiratory disease?
o: For all dogs with any cough, as first-line treatment on the day of intake
For a severe or debilitating dry cough with antibiotic cover, and not if pneumonia is suspected
For dogs with a productive cough, fever and an inflammatory leukogram
e: Antitussives are reserved for severe non-productive cough with antibiotic cover, and avoided with an inflammatory leukogram, fever or consolidation.

q: Which pathogens are long shedders, warranting caution before mixing recovered dogs with susceptible dogs?
o: Canine distemper virus, H3N2 canine influenza virus, Bordetella and Mycoplasma
Canine adenovirus-2, canine respiratory coronavirus and canine parainfluenza virus
Streptococcus zooepidemicus, canine parainfluenza virus and canine respiratory coronavirus
e: CDV, CIV H3N2, Bordetella and Mycoplasma have prolonged shedding, so caution is needed before mixing recovered dogs with susceptible ones.

q: Which antibiotics should be first line for shelter canine respiratory disease under stewardship principles?
o: Enrofloxacin or azithromycin, keeping doxycycline for culture-confirmed resistant disease
Doxycycline or amoxicillin-clavulanate, keeping macrolides and fluoroquinolones for culture-confirmed resistant disease
Cefovecin as a single injection for all dogs, keeping oral drugs for treatment failures
e: First-line therapy is doxycycline or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Macrolides and fluoroquinolones are reserved for culture-confirmed resistant lower-airway disease.

q: How is canine influenza virus classified, and how are its subtypes defined?
o: As an influenza A virus, with subtypes defined by haemagglutinin and neuraminidase proteins (H3N8 and H3N2)
As an influenza B virus, with subtypes defined by internal matrix proteins (H1N1 and H3N2)
As a paramyxovirus, with subtypes defined by fusion proteins (H3N8 and H5N1)
e: CIV is an enveloped RNA influenza A virus. Subtypes are defined by the H and N surface glycoproteins, and the canine subtypes are H3N8 and H3N2.

q: Which feature is notable about the H3N2 canine influenza virus subtype?
o: Equine origin and infection of dogs only
Avian origin and a broader host range, including cats
Human origin and infection of dogs only
e: H3N2 is of avian origin (Korea 2007, US 2015), with a wider host range than the dog-only H3N8.

q: Which statement about the timing of canine influenza virus infection and shedding is correct?
o: Incubation is 2 to 5 days, and peak shedding occurs 2 to 4 days after infection, before signs, so healthy-looking dogs can be contagious.
Incubation is 10 to 14 days, and peak shedding occurs once coughing begins, so healthy-looking dogs are not contagious.
Incubation is 1 day, and peak shedding occurs 3 weeks after infection, when antibody is first detectable.
e: Incubation is 2 to 5 days, with peak shedding at 2 to 4 days that overlaps incubation. About 10 to 20% of infected dogs are subclinical shedders, so all exposed dogs are a risk.

q: Regarding a carrier state, which statement is correct for canine influenza virus?
o: There is no true carrier state; once shedding stops the dog is no longer contagious.
Recovered dogs become lifelong carriers that intermittently shed the virus.
Carriers are common and shed virus for about 6 months after recovery.
e: CIV has no true carrier state. Once replication and shedding cease, the dog is no longer contagious, although H3N2 shedding can be prolonged.

q: Which pattern best describes the disease caused by canine influenza virus?
o: High morbidity and low mortality, with severe disease usually due to co-infection or comorbidity
Low morbidity and high mortality, with most infected dogs dying of viral pneumonia
High morbidity and high mortality, with most deaths occurring in the first 48 hours
e: CIV is high morbidity and low mortality. Pneumonia-related fatality is about 5 to 8%, and severe disease usually reflects co-infection or comorbidity.

q: How is canine influenza managed in a shelter dog?
o: With supportive care, antibiotics only for secondary bacterial infection or pneumonia, and antitussives avoided with a productive cough
With an antiviral drug in all dogs and routine broad-spectrum antibiotics from the first day
With antitussives for all dogs and antibiotics only if the dog is still coughing after 3 weeks
e: Care is supportive. Antibiotics target secondary bacterial infection or pneumonia, and antitussives have little evidence and are contraindicated with a productive cough.

q: Which statement about the environmental control of canine influenza virus, compared with parvovirus, is correct?
o: It is harder, because it survives for over a year and resists all common disinfectants.
It is the same, because both are non-enveloped viruses that survive for years in the environment.
It is easier, because it is an enveloped virus surviving about 24 to 48 hours on non-porous surfaces and readily inactivated by standard disinfectants.
e: As an enveloped virus, CIV survives about 24 to 48 hours on non-porous surfaces, 8 to 12 hours on porous surfaces and minutes on hands, and is readily inactivated by accelerated hydrogen peroxide, bleach, quaternary ammonium and potassium peroxymonosulfate.

q: Once canine influenza is suspected in a shelter, how should the exposed dogs be managed?
o: Treat only coughing dogs as exposed, quarantine for 3 days, and release them once coughing stops.
Treat all dogs as protected if vaccinated, and quarantine only unvaccinated dogs for 7 days.
Treat all dogs present as exposed, quarantine for at least 14 days, and release negatives after PCR on days 4 to 7.
e: High transmissibility and pre-clinical shedding mean all dogs present should be treated as exposed. Quarantine is a minimum of 14 days, with PCR at days 4 to 7 to release negatives.

q: Which swab type should be used to collect a sample for canine influenza PCR?
o: A synthetic polyester or dacron swab on a plastic shaft
A cotton-tipped swab on a wooden shaft
A calcium alginate swab on an aluminium shaft only
e: Cotton fatty acids and wood resins or tannins inhibit PCR and viral assays, so polyester or dacron swabs on plastic or aluminium shafts are used.

q: Why do dogs imported from South Korea or China warrant extra precautions for canine influenza virus?
o: High regional H3N8 prevalence, which justifies immediate vaccination and release
High regional H3N2 prevalence, which justifies a 14-day quarantine and testing
Lack of any vaccine, which justifies refusal to accept the dog
e: High regional H3N2 prevalence justifies an aggressive 14-day quarantine and testing for imports from these areas.

q: What is a key limitation of immunity after recovery from canine influenza?
o: Protection lasts only a few days, so recovered dogs are quickly re-infected.
Protection is strain-specific, and rapid mutation limits cross-protection.
Protection is complete and lifelong against all subtypes.
e: Post-infection antibody persists 5 to 6 years but is strain-specific, and rapid mutation limits cross-protection.

q: Which is the most important feline dermatophyte, and what do spores need to establish infection?
o: Trichophyton mentagrophytes (over 90% of feline cases), with spores needing intact skin
Microsporum canis (over 90% of feline cases), with spores needing skin microtrauma
Microsporum gypseum (over 90% of feline cases), with spores needing deep puncture wounds
e: M. canis causes over 90% of feline dermatophytosis. Spores need microtrauma, such as humidity maceration or parasites, to breach the skin defences and infect the follicle.

q: Which statement about immunity to and transmission of dermatophytosis is correct?
o: Recovery depends on antibody titres, and spread is by the airborne route only.
Recovery depends on cell-mediated immunity, and spread is by contact, fomites and occasionally fleas.
Recovery is spontaneous in all cats, and spread is by direct contact only.
e: Protection is cell mediated, so antibody titres are clinically useless. Spread is by contact, contaminated fomites and occasionally fleas, and staff can mechanically move spores between cats.

q: Which statement about the incubation and environmental persistence of dermatophytes is correct?
o: Incubation is 24 to 48 hours, so a 3-day quarantine is enough, and spores die within a day.
Incubation is 2 to 4 months, so a 90-day quarantine is required, and spores persist for a year.
Incubation is 2 to 4 weeks, so watch-and-wait quarantine is impractical, and spores persist for weeks to months.
e: The long incubation makes quarantining exposed animals simply to watch for lesions impractical, and active screening is preferred. Spores remain infectious for weeks to months unless the area is thoroughly cleaned.

q: In dogs, lesions that look like classic ringworm are more often caused by
o: Microsporum canis infection.
bacterial pyoderma or demodicosis.
sarcoptic mange.
e: Ringworm-looking lesions in dogs are more commonly pyoderma or demodicosis than true dermatophytosis.

q: Which test is the gold standard for diagnosing ringworm in shelter cats, and how is it collected?
o: Fungal culture on dermatophyte test medium, collected by the toothbrush technique
A Wood's lamp examination, collected by the tape-strip technique
Direct microscopy of hairs, collected by fine-needle aspiration
e: Fungal culture on dermatophyte test medium is the gold standard, typically via the toothbrush technique. Direct microscopy can show ectothrix spores on hairs.

q: In a P-score system for dermatophyte culture, how should a P3 cat be managed?
o: It is removed from the general population for strict isolation and full treatment.
It is treated as a fomite carrier and dipped once before adoption.
It is re-cultured in a week and moved to the adoption floor if the result is lower.
e: The P-score is a colony count (P1 is 1 to 4, P2 is 5 to 9, P3 is 10 or more colony-forming units per plate). P3 cats have high counts and confirmed infection, so they need isolation and full treatment.

q: In dermatophyte culture screening, by when are over 95% of positive cultures identified, and how long are cultures held?
o: By day 10 to 14, with cultures (not animals) held for the full 21 days
By day 3 to 5, with cultures held for the full 7 days
By day 21 to 28, with animals held for the full 28 days
e: Most positives appear by day 10 to 14, and day 10 is a key read point. Cultures, not animals, are held for 21 days to detect slower Trichophyton.

q: How is mycological cure defined in shelter ringworm management?
o: Three consecutive weekly negative cultures, or two if lime sulfur and continuous oral itraconazole were used
One negative culture at least 2 weeks after the last treatment
Complete hair regrowth and a negative Wood's lamp examination
e: Three consecutive weekly negative cultures define cure. Two suffice only with combined lime sulfur and continuous oral itraconazole.

q: Which disinfectant regimen is effective against ringworm spores after mechanical removal of hair and debris?
o: Bleach at 1:32 for 10 minutes, or 1% potassium peroxymonosulfate
Quaternary ammonium or chlorhexidine at label dilution
Bleach at 1:10, accelerated hydrogen peroxide at 1:16, or 2% potassium peroxymonosulfate
e: Ringworm needs stronger regimens than most viruses: bleach at 1:10, accelerated hydrogen peroxide at 1:16 or 2% potassium peroxymonosulfate. Bleach at 1:32 for 10 minutes suffices for parvovirus and other viruses, and 1% potassium peroxymonosulfate is unreliable for spores. Quaternary ammonium and chlorhexidine are ineffective.

q: What is the cornerstone of environmental decontamination in a ringworm outbreak?
o: Fogging the room with a disinfectant and leaving it closed for 24 hours
Repeated disinfection with a quaternary ammonium product without prior cleaning
Mechanical removal of spores and hair by vacuuming, sweeping or damp dusting before disinfection
e: Mechanical removal is the single most critical step. Disinfect only after thorough cleaning.

q: Which description of feline panleukopenia virus is correct?
o: A non-enveloped single-stranded DNA parvovirus that enters cells through the transferrin receptor and infects rapidly dividing cells
An enveloped RNA coronavirus that enters cells through the ACE2 receptor and infects the respiratory epithelium
A non-enveloped RNA calicivirus that enters cells through the junctional adhesion molecule and infects oral mucosa
e: FPV is a non-enveloped single-stranded DNA parvovirus with one serotype. It uses the transferrin receptor and needs the S phase of division, targeting marrow, lymphoid tissue, intestinal crypts and fetal or neonatal tissue.

q: What causes the leukopenia of feline panleukopenia virus infection?
o: Immune-mediated destruction of circulating leukocytes
Sequestration of leukocytes in the spleen after splenic enlargement
Marrow suppression, neutrophil loss into the damaged gut and lymphoid depletion
e: Marrow suppression, neutrophil loss into the damaged gut and lymphoid depletion together cause the panleukopenia.

q: Which statement about the transmission and survival of feline panleukopenia virus is correct?
o: It spreads faecal-orally (directly or by fomites), crosses the placenta in mid-gestation, and survives in the environment for over a year.
It spreads by aerosol only, does not cross the placenta, and survives in the environment for about 48 hours.
It spreads by flea bites only, crosses the placenta in late gestation, and survives in the environment for 2 weeks.
e: Faecal-oral spread is primary, and fetal infection occurs in mid-gestation. FPV is exceptionally hardy, infective for around 13 months and persisting over a year in organic matter.

q: A 4-month-old kitten was healthy at night and is found dead in the morning. Panleukopenia is suspected. Which form of the disease does this represent?
o: The acute form, which typically causes a biphasic fever and death within 2 weeks
The peracute form, which kills kittens under 6 months within hours and can be mistaken for poisoning
The subacute form, which causes chronic weight loss over several months
e: Peracute disease kills kittens in hours (lethargy to coma to death) and resembles poisoning, with near-100% mortality. The acute form, with biphasic fever, vomiting and diarrhoea, is the most common.

q: Which finding indicates a very guarded prognosis in feline panleukopenia, and which bacterium is the most serious secondary invader?
o: A persistent white blood cell count under 2000/microlitre, with E. coli
A white blood cell count of 8000/microlitre, with Staphylococcus aureus
A packed cell volume of 35%, with Clostridium tetani
e: A white blood cell count persistently under 2000/microlitre carries a very guarded prognosis. E. coli is the worst secondary invader once the gut barrier fails.

q: Which statement about supportive treatment in feline panleukopenia is correct?
o: Transfuse red cells only when the packed cell volume is under 25%, and give metoclopramide as the first-line antiemetic.
Avoid all blood products because of the DIC risk, and give phenothiazines as the first-line antiemetic.
Transfuse plasma or whole blood when plasma protein is under 2 g/dL or the white cell count is under 2000/microlitre, and avoid metoclopramide.
e: Whole blood or plasma at 20 mL/kg/day is indicated when plasma protein is under 2 g/dL or white cell count under 2000/microlitre. Metoclopramide is avoided in cats, and maropitant or ondansetron is preferred.

q: What is the role of feline recombinant interferon-omega in panleukopenia?
o: It inhibits the virus in culture but has not changed clinical signs or survival, so it is not cost-effective for routine shelter use.
It reduces mortality by more than half and is recommended for every case.
It replaces the need for fluid therapy in mildly affected kittens.
e: It inhibits FPV in cell culture but has not changed signs or survival, so it is not cost-effective for routine shelter use.

q: Which set of agents reliably inactivates feline panleukopenia virus?
o: Bleach, potassium peroxymonosulfate, accelerated hydrogen peroxide and calcium hypochlorite
Quaternary ammonium compounds, alcohol, chlorhexidine and phenols
Alcohol, quaternary ammonium compounds, bleach and chlorhexidine
e: Bleach, KPMS, AHP and calcium hypochlorite work, after removing organic matter. Quaternary ammonium compounds and alcohol are ineffective against this hardy non-enveloped virus.

q: Which cats are in the high-risk exposed category during a panleukopenia outbreak, and is quarantining healthy unexposed cats recommended?
o: Only cats with diarrhoea; all healthy unexposed cats should be quarantined for 14 days.
Kittens under 4 months and unvaccinated cats; routine quarantine of healthy unexposed cats is not recommended.
Only cats over 5 months old; quarantine is required for all kittens.
e: Kittens under 4 months (some say 5) and unvaccinated cats are high risk. Low risk is over 5 months and vaccinated 5 to 7 days before. Prolonged length of stay is itself a risk factor.

q: What is the standard shelter panleukopenia vaccine, and what kind of immunity does it produce?
o: A killed FVRCP given intranasally, producing partial immunity
A canine DAPP vaccine given subcutaneously, producing sterilising immunity
MLV FVRCP given subcutaneously, producing sterilising immunity
e: MLV FVRCP given SC is the shelter standard, with fast onset and better ability than killed vaccine to override maternal antibody. Unlike most respiratory agents, FPV vaccine produces sterilising immunity.

q: During an FPV outbreak, what booster should exposed unvaccinated adult cats receive?
o: Canine DAPP, unless vaccinated in the previous 14 days
Killed FVRCP, unless vaccinated in the previous 6 months
MLV FVRCP, unless vaccinated in the previous 14 days
e: Cats receive MLV FVRCP, not the canine DAPP, and exposed adults are boosted unless they were vaccinated in the previous 14 days.

q: How long does passive immunisation with anti-FPV (or hyperimmune CPV) serum protect a kitten, and what follows?
o: About 6 months, with active vaccination given on the same day
About 2 to 4 weeks, with active vaccination delayed 3 to 4 weeks afterwards
About 24 hours, with active vaccination given immediately afterwards
e: Passive serum gives 2 to 4 weeks of protection, and active vaccination is delayed 3 to 4 weeks to avoid neutralisation of the vaccine.

q: What are the expected mortality of kittens with feline panleukopenia and the immunity after natural recovery?
o: Kitten mortality under 10%, and immunity lasting about 6 months after recovery
Kitten mortality over 90% (peaking at 3 to 5 months), and lifelong immunity after recovery
Kitten mortality of about 50%, and no immunity after recovery
e: Kitten mortality exceeds 90%, peaking at 3 to 5 months as maternal immunity wanes. Recovery confers lifelong immunity, and a single serotype means broad, durable protection.

q: How are FeLV and FIV classified, and are they zoonotic?
o: FeLV is a gammaretrovirus and FIV is a lentivirus, both in the family Retroviridae, and neither is zoonotic.
FeLV is a lentivirus and FIV is a gammaretrovirus, and both are zoonotic to immunocompromised people.
Both are herpesviruses, and neither is zoonotic.
e: Both are retroviruses. FeLV is a gammaretrovirus (oncornavirus) and FIV is a lentivirus. Neither is zoonotic.

q: What are the three outcomes of FeLV infection?
o: Acute, subacute and chronic
Latent, reactivated and cleared
Abortive, regressive and progressive
e: FeLV resolves to abortive (cleared), regressive (provirus latent in marrow) or progressive (systemic infection with shedding).

q: Which pattern of test results is typical of abortive FeLV infection?
o: Antigen and immunofluorescent antibody positive, PCR negative
Antigen, immunofluorescent antibody and PCR all negative
Antigen negative, immunofluorescent antibody positive, PCR positive
e: A robust immune response clears the virus before dissemination, so antigen, IFA and PCR are all negative. Antibody is the only positive marker.

q: Which pairing of virus and primary transmission route is correct?
o: FeLV by oronasal social contact and nursing, and FIV by deep bite wounds
FeLV by deep bite wounds, and FIV by oronasal social contact and nursing
FeLV by flea bites, and FIV by faecal-oral spread
e: FeLV is the friendly-cat virus, spread by grooming, shared dishes and nursing. FIV is the fighting-cat virus, spread by deep bite wounds. Compatible non-aggressive cats can cohabit with little FIV risk.

q: Which statement about the clinical signs of feline retroviral infection is correct?
o: There are no pathognomonic signs, and many cats are asymptomatic for long periods.
Chronic gingivitis is pathognomonic for FIV, and mediastinal lymphoma is pathognomonic for FeLV.
Infected cats always show weight loss and lymphadenopathy within 6 months of infection.
e: Disease comes from chronic effects (anaemia, neoplasia, inflammation and opportunistic infection). FeLV can also cause fading kitten syndrome in neonates.

q: Which sample gives the most sensitive point-of-care FeLV antigen result, and what do the point-of-care tests detect?
o: Whole blood; they detect FeLV p27 antigen and FIV antibody.
Serum; they detect FeLV antibody and FIV p24 antigen.
Plasma; they detect FeLV and FIV proviral DNA.
e: Point-of-care tests detect FeLV p27 antigen and FIV antibody, and whole blood is more sensitive than serum or plasma for p27.

q: How does the immunofluorescent antibody (IFA) test for FeLV differ between regressive and progressive infection?
o: It is negative in regressive infection and positive in progressive infection.
It is positive in regressive infection and negative in progressive infection.
It is positive in both, but with a higher titre in regressive infection.
e: IFA detects p27 in leukocyte and platelet cytoplasm, so it is negative in regressive infection and positive in progressive (marrow-infected) disease.

q: A low proviral copy number on quantitative FeLV PCR indicates
o: progressive infection with high morbidity.
abortive infection with no risk of reactivation.
regressive infection with prolonged survival.
e: A low copy number marks regressive infection with prolonged survival, while a high copy number marks progressive infection with higher morbidity and mortality.

q: Which practice is appropriate for preventing FeLV and FIV transmission in a shelter?
o: Testing each cat individually, and avoiding transfusion of untested blood or cross-contaminated invasive instruments
Testing pooled samples from each cage, and disinfecting the air handling system weekly
Testing one cat per room as a proxy for the group, and quarantining the room for 30 days
e: Both viruses are fragile and are not airborne or spread by casual handling, but they transmit efficiently by transfusion and contaminated invasive instruments. Pooling lowers sensitivity, and proxy testing is invalid.

q: What must be established before a cat enters group housing, and is FIV testing required?
o: A negative FIV result; FeLV testing may be optional if the cats are compatible and stress is low.
A negative FeLV result; FIV testing may be optional if the cats are compatible and stress is low.
Negative results for both FeLV and FIV, together with a recent fecal PCR.
e: A negative FeLV result is required before group housing. FIV testing may be optional if the cats are compatible and stress is low.

q: How is the FeLV vaccine best described, and why is it given low on the left hind limb?
o: Non-core for at-risk cats, so status is tested first, and the site allows amputation with clean margins if a sarcoma develops
Core for all cats, so it is given at intake, and the site allows easy access to the vaccine in fractious cats
Non-core and given only to FeLV-positive cats, and the site avoids interference with the FIV vaccine
e: The vaccine is non-core for at-risk cats: determine status first, then give 2 doses 3 to 4 weeks apart from 8 weeks. Distal-limb placement means an adjuvant-associated injection-site sarcoma can be excised with clean margins.

q: What is the recommendation on FIV vaccination in shelters?
o: It is recommended for all cats, because it prevents infection in more than 95% of vaccinated cats.
It is not recommended, because it covers only subtypes A and D and induces antibody that is indistinguishable from infection on common tests.
It is recommended only for FIV-positive cats, because it lowers their viral load.
e: FIV vaccine is non-core and not recommended in shelters, as it covers only subtypes A and D and induces antibody that point-of-care tests cannot distinguish from infection.

q: Are epidemic outbreaks of FeLV or FIV expected in a shelter, and how do the viruses affect lifespan?
o: Yes, both spread rapidly by aerosol; FIV shortens lifespan, and FeLV is often normal.
Yes, both spread rapidly by fomites; both shorten lifespan to under 1 year.
No, because both are chronic low-transmission infections; FeLV typically shortens lifespan, and FIV is variable and often normal.
e: Both are chronic, low-transmission infections, so epidemics are not expected and management focuses on testing and segregation. FeLV typically shortens lifespan, whereas FIV is frequently normal.

q: Which statement about the cause of feline infectious peritonitis is correct?
o: It is caused by a separate coronavirus that spreads between cats by aerosol.
It is caused by a herpesvirus that reactivates during stress.
It follows internal mutation of enteric coronavirus to a macrophage-tropic virus within an individual cat, commonly involving the spike gene.
e: FIP is a complication of feline coronavirus, a large enveloped RNA alphacoronavirus prone to mutation. The internal mutation theory holds that FECV mutates to macrophage-tropic FIPV within an individual cat, commonly in the S gene and 3c, 7a and 7b.

q: Which immune profile results in effusive (wet) FIP?
o: A strong humoral response with weak or absent cellular immunity, causing immune-complex vasculitis
A strong cell-mediated response with weak humoral immunity, causing granulomatous vasculitis
A balanced humoral and cellular response that clears the virus but damages the pleura
e: Strong humoral plus weak cellular immunity produces immune-complex vasculitis (type III hypersensitivity) and effusion. A strong cell-mediated response can prevent disease.

q: Which statement about coronavirus infection in cats is correct?
o: Under 3% of seropositive cats develop FIP, enteric coronavirus spreads faecal-orally by shared litter boxes, and kittens 8 to 16 weeks shed far more virus than adults.
Most seropositive cats develop FIP, coronavirus spreads by aerosol, and adults shed more virus than kittens.
About 25% of seropositive cats develop FIP, coronavirus spreads by fleas, and shedding is equal in all ages.
e: FIP is uncommon: under 3% of seropositive cats develop it. FECV spreads oronasally through faeces, especially shared litter boxes, and kittens 8 to 16 weeks shed about 10,000 times more than adults.

q: Is FIP contagious between cats, and how should a cluster of cases in a shelter be interpreted?
o: FIPV spreads readily by the faecal-oral route, and a cluster indicates a highly contagious mutant virus.
FIPV spreads by aerosol between cats, and a cluster indicates that ventilation has failed.
The FIPV itself is essentially non-contagious, and a cluster reflects conditions that amplify coronavirus load and host risk.
e: FIPV has lost epithelial tropism, so it is not spread faecal-orally and is essentially non-contagious. A shelter cluster reflects husbandry and housing that create high FCoV loads.

q: Why does the RT-PCR plus S-gene mutation assay have high specificity but low sensitivity for FIP?
o: The assay detects antibody rather than virus, so early infections are missed.
The assay works only on faecal samples, so effusion samples give false negatives.
The mutation is an individual variable event, so novel changes escape the primers, and it misses Type II coronavirus.
e: FIP mutations are individual and variable, so novel point mutations escape the S-gene primers, and the assay does not capture Type II feline coronavirus.

q: What is the definitive antemortem diagnostic test for FIP?
o: A serum coronavirus antibody titre above 1:1600
Faecal coronavirus RT-PCR on three consecutive days
Immunohistochemistry showing coronavirus antigen within macrophages in pyogranulomatous lesions
e: Demonstrating viral antigen inside macrophages within classic lesions (immunohistochemistry or direct immunofluorescence) is the gold standard, ruling out bystander enteric coronavirus.

q: Which statement about the clinical forms of FIP is correct?
o: FIP presents as effusive (wet) or non-effusive (dry), often with mixed features, and neurological disease occurs mainly in the non-effusive form.
FIP presents only as an effusive form, and neurological disease occurs mainly in kittens under 8 weeks.
FIP presents as effusive or non-effusive, and ocular lesions occur only in the effusive form.
e: The form reflects the immune response. Neurological disease is mainly a non-effusive manifestation, and ocular lesions (uveitis, retinitis, keratic precipitates) occur in both forms.

q: Which description matches a classic FIP effusion?
o: Straw yellow, viscous, high in protein, frothing when shaken, and of low cellularity
Serosanguineous, watery, low in protein and of high cellularity with bacteria
Milky white and opaque, with a triglyceride concentration higher than serum
e: A classic FIP effusion is a modified transudate or non-septic exudate: straw yellow, viscous, protein over 3.5 g/dL, low cellularity, and frothing on shaking.

q: Which statement about the albumin:globulin (A:G) ratio of a cat effusion is correct?
o: An A:G ratio over 1 has about 89% positive predictive value for FIP, and a ratio under 0.5 has about 91% negative predictive value.
The A:G ratio has no diagnostic value in cats and should not be used.
An A:G ratio under 0.5 has about 89% positive predictive value for FIP, and a ratio over 1 has about 91% negative predictive value.
e: An effusion A:G under 0.5 has about 89% positive predictive value for FIP, and a ratio over 1 has about 91% negative predictive value.

q: Which statement about the treatment of FIP is correct?
o: Untreated FIP resolves in most cats, and prednisolone plus cyclophosphamide cures the disease.
Untreated FIP is nearly always fatal, and modern antivirals are GS-441524 (a nucleoside analogue) and GC376 (a protease inhibitor).
Untreated FIP is fatal in about 30% of cats, and remdesivir has no role in treatment.
e: Untreated FIP is nearly always fatal once signs appear. Historical prednisolone and cyclophosphamide only slow progression. GS-441524 and GC376 are the antivirals, and remdesivir is the GS-441524 prodrug.

q: Because feline coronavirus is enveloped, how should shelter sanitation approach it, and how long can it survive dry?
o: Only bleach inactivates it and rooms are closed for 8 weeks; it can survive over a year dry.
Standard disinfectants inactivate it and rooms are reused promptly; it can survive up to about 7 weeks dry.
Only steam inactivates it and rooms are closed for 4 weeks; it survives less than a day dry.
e: Enveloped FCoV is readily inactivated by standard shelter disinfectants, so rooms are cleaned and reused promptly. It survives up to about 7 weeks dry, which underpins the conservative 2-month wait before introducing a new cat to a home where a cat with FIP lived.

q: How is an FIP outbreak defined in a shelter of genetically unrelated cats, compared with a breeding cattery?
o: Incidence over 10% in the shelter, and over 1% in the cattery
Incidence over 25% in both settings
Incidence over 1% in the shelter, and over 10% in the cattery
e: In an unrelated shelter population, over 1% is an outbreak. Related, densely housed cattery cats tolerate a higher baseline, so the cattery threshold is over 10% (hoarding 5 to 10%).

q: Which approach is the cornerstone of managing an FIP outbreak, and is vaccination useful?
o: Risk assessment, reduction of environmental load and a clean break; the intranasal vaccine shows minimal efficacy.
Mass PCR testing of all cats; the intranasal vaccine gives sterilising immunity.
Vaccination of all cats twice yearly; mass euthanasia of seropositive cats.
e: Management is risk assessment, lowering environmental FCoV load, and a clean break between affected and new populations. Mass PCR is not useful, and the intranasal FIP vaccine has minimal efficacy.

q: Which age group is at greatest risk of FIP?
o: Cats up to 3 years old, especially 4 to 16 months
Cats over 10 years old
Cats between 5 and 8 years old
e: Risk concentrates under 3 years, especially 4 to 16 months. In an Australian series, 80% of cases were under 2 years.

q: Where does feline herpesvirus-1 establish latency, and what proportion of infected cats become carriers?
o: In the dorsal root ganglia, with about 10% of infected cats becoming carriers
In the trigeminal ganglia, with at least 80% of infected cats becoming lifelong carriers
In the tonsils, with all infected cats clearing the virus within 6 months
e: FHV-1 becomes latent in the trigeminal ganglia and cool upper respiratory tissues and reactivates with stress. At least 80% of infected cats become lifelong latent carriers.

q: How is feline calicivirus best described?
o: A non-enveloped RNA virus with many antigenically distinct strains within one serotype
An enveloped RNA virus with several distinct serotypes that require separate vaccines
A non-enveloped DNA virus with a single strain that is easily inactivated
e: FCV is a non-enveloped, rapidly mutating single-stranded RNA virus, with one serotype but many antigenically distinct strains.

q: How does Bordetella bronchiseptica predispose a cat to co-infection?
o: By destroying respiratory cilia, removing a key mucosal defence
By suppressing the bone marrow, causing neutropenia
By forming latent infection in the trigeminal ganglia
e: Bordetella destroys respiratory cilia, removing a key mucosal defence and predisposing to secondary infection.

q: Which statement about the spread of feline upper respiratory disease in shelters is correct?
o: Airborne spread is the most common route, droplets travel over 10 m (33 ft), and stress does not affect viral shedding.
Direct contact is the only route, droplets travel over 3 m (10 ft), and biosecurity can eliminate all new cases.
Fomites are the most common route, droplets travel about 1 to 1.3 m (3.3 to 4.3 ft), and stress can reactivate herpesvirus even with flawless biosecurity.
e: Fomite transmission dominates, except for herpesvirus recrudescence. Sneezed droplets travel about 1 to 1.3 m, so facing cage banks should be at least 1.3 m (4.3 ft) apart. Stress-induced recrudescence means new cases arise even with flawless biosecurity.

q: How does feline upper respiratory disease relate to ventilation?
o: It is not airborne, so good air quality matters but separate per-cage ventilation is not required.
It is airborne, so each cage needs a separate air handler.
It is airborne only in cats housed within 6 ft of each other.
e: Feline upper respiratory disease is not airborne. Good air quality matters, but separate per-cage ventilation is not required.

q: How long do feline herpesvirus-1 and feline calicivirus survive in the environment?
o: Herpesvirus survives at least 28 days, whereas calicivirus survives about 18 hours.
Both survive for at least 6 months on dry surfaces.
Herpesvirus survives about 18 hours in damp conditions, whereas calicivirus survives at least 28 days at room temperature.
e: FHV-1 is fragile and easily disinfected, whereas FCV is hardy, surviving at least 28 days at room temperature, which drives fomite spread.

q: Which findings point to feline herpesvirus-1 keratitis and to Chlamydia felis, respectively?
o: Tongue ulcers, and dendritic corneal ulcers
Chemosis with conjunctivitis, and tongue ulcers
Dendritic corneal ulcers, and chemosis progressing from unilateral serous to bilateral mucopurulent conjunctivitis
e: Dendritic corneal ulceration is characteristic of FHV-1 keratitis. Chemosis with conjunctivitis progressing from unilateral serous to bilateral mucopurulent suggests Chlamydia felis.

q: Which antiviral and dose is used for feline herpesvirus-1 disease?
o: Famciclovir 90 mg/kg PO every 8 hours
Acyclovir 10 mg/kg PO every 12 hours
Oseltamivir 2 mg/kg PO every 12 hours
e: High-dose famciclovir (90 mg/kg PO every 8 hours) outperforms low dose for FHV-1, and topical idoxuridine or cidofovir treats keratitis. Acyclovir is not recommended in cats.

q: How should doxycycline be given to a cat to prevent oesophageal stricture?
o: As a tablet given dry, followed by a short period of fasting
As a liquid, or as a tablet followed by a water or food flush
As a tablet crushed into a small amount of dry food
e: Doxycycline hyclate tablets can lodge in the feline oesophagus and cause strictures, so the liquid is used or the dose is followed by water or food.

q: Doxycycline is being considered for a 3-week-old kitten with Mycoplasma felis-associated upper respiratory disease. What is the correct approach?
o: It can be used safely under 4 weeks, because tetracycline enamel discolouration is cosmetic only in cats.
It is contraindicated under 12 weeks, because of permanent growth defects in developing bone.
It is contraindicated under 8 weeks, because of nephrotoxicity in neonates.
