e: Doxycycline is labelled for cats over 4 weeks, but it can be used safely below that age, since the enamel-staining effect of tetracyclines is cosmetic only in cats.

q: Streptococcus canis and Streptococcus zooepidemicus in cats are best distinguished by
o: S. zooepidemicus causing necrotising fasciitis, and S. canis being part of routine feline PCR panels.
S. canis being non-zoonotic, and S. zooepidemicus being zoonotic.
S. canis causing outbreak necrotising sinusitis, meningitis or necrotising fasciitis, and S. zooepidemicus needing a special PCR request.
e: They are distinct Gram-positive species. S. canis can cause outbreak necrotising disease with up to 30% fatality, and S. zooepidemicus is excluded from routine feline PCR panels. Both are zoonotic.

q: A cat on a dairy farm develops depressed mentation, ataxia, blindness and oculonasal discharge after exposure to raw milk from sick cows. What should be considered?
o: H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza
Feline panleukopenia virus
Feline calicivirus
e: Severe neurological signs plus farm and raw milk exposure should raise suspicion for H5N1, which caused severe, often fatal disease in farm cats during the 2024 to 2025 US outbreak.

q: Which age group is most susceptible to Chlamydia felis infection?
o: Adult cats aged 3 to 5 years
Geriatric cats over 10 years of age
Kittens around 5 to 12 weeks of age
e: Chlamydia felis disease is seen most often in kittens around 5 to 12 weeks old, and susceptibility decreases with age.

q: Daily spot cleaning of a cat's own housing unit is
o: acceptable in all cases, including suspected calicivirus, because it reduces stress.
never acceptable in shelters, because a full clean is required every day.
acceptable for routine upper respiratory cases and healthy cats, but insufficient once calicivirus is suspected.
e: Spot cleaning reduces stress and is fine for routine cases. Suspected FCV contamination needs a fuller protocol with disinfectants effective against the resistant virus (1:32 bleach, potassium peroxymonosulfate or AHP).

q: What is the labelled dose of transdermal mirtazapine for feline appetite stimulation?
o: 2 mg/kg once daily, calculated from body weight
0.5 mg/kg every 72 hours, calculated from body weight
A fixed 2 mg per cat once daily, regardless of body weight
e: Mirataz is dosed as a fixed 2 mg per cat (a 1.5-inch ribbon on the inner pinna), not by weight.

q: A cat with upper respiratory disease has not responded to treatment after 5 to 7 days. What does this indicate?
o: The need for further diagnostic work-up
That the antibiotic dose should be doubled
That the cat should be isolated for a further 6 weeks
e: Lack of response within 5 to 7 days suggests an additional medical or drug-related problem needing further work-up.

q: Which hygiene measures are effective against feline calicivirus?
o: 1:32 bleach, potassium peroxymonosulfate or accelerated hydrogen peroxide, with soap-and-water handwashing
Quaternary ammonium products and alcohol-based hand sanitiser
Alcohol-based hand sanitiser and chlorhexidine wipes
e: Non-enveloped FCV resists quaternary ammonium and alcohol. Use 1:32 bleach, KPMS or AHP for surfaces, and soap and water or AHP wipes for hands.

q: Which measure lowers the clinical upper respiratory disease rate in shelter cats?
o: Rotating staff between sections daily, using large groups, and housing young kittens in the shelter
Separating staff by section, keeping groups small and stable (5 or fewer), and sending kittens too young for adoption directly to foster
Housing cats in regrouped cohorts each week to build immunity, and using a single cleaning team
e: Dedicating staff by section, keeping groups small and stable (regrouping is linked to herpesvirus reactivation), and sending kittens too young for adoption to foster all reduce upper respiratory disease.

q: Is routine vaccination of shelter cats against Bordetella and Chlamydia recommended?
o: No; core MLV FVRCP is given at intake, but Bordetella and Chlamydia vaccination is not recommended routinely.
Yes; both vaccines are core and given at intake to all cats.
Yes; both vaccines are given only to cats that show signs of respiratory disease.
e: Routine Bordetella and Chlamydia vaccination is not recommended for shelter cats, whereas core MLV FVRCP is given at intake.

q: A dog imported from Mexico has a history of late-term abortion. A rapid slide agglutination test for Brucella canis in the clinic is positive. What is the correct next step?
o: Euthanise the dog immediately, because a positive result confirms infection.
Spay the dog and begin doxycycline and rifampin without further testing.
Isolate the dog and confirm with agar gel immunodiffusion, culture or PCR before deciding disposition.
e: The rapid slide agglutination test has a high false-positive rate, so isolation is required but disposition needs confirmation. B. canis is zoonotic and not reliably cleared by treatment.

q: Which statement about Brucella canis transmission in a shelter is correct?
o: It is spread by aerosol between dogs housed in the same ward, so all dogs in the ward are exposed.
It is spread only by ticks, so tick control alone prevents shelter transmission.
Transmission needs contact with infectious secretions (semen, vaginal discharge, aborted material, urine); it is not airborne under typical shelter conditions.
e: B. canis is not airborne. Transmission needs direct contact with reproductive secretions, aborted material or blood. It is zoonotic, so staff who handled aborted fetuses or discharge should see occupational health.

q: Which diagnostic test is the gold standard for detecting Mycoplasma haemofelis infection?
o: Examination of a stained blood smear
Faecal flotation
PCR on blood for haemoplasma
e: PCR is the most sensitive and specific test and can speciate. Blood smear sensitivity is low, because parasitaemia is cyclic.

q: Which statement about Mycoplasma haemofelis and flea control in shelters is correct?
o: Ticks are the primary vector, so tick control is the most important prevention measure.
Cat fleas are the primary vector, so strict flea control is the most important prevention measure.
Faecal-oral transmission is the primary route, so litter management is the most important measure.
e: Ctenocephalides felis is the primary vector for M. haemofelis, so flea-free status substantially reduces transmission. Blood donor cats must also be PCR screened.

q: An unvaccinated 8-week-old puppy presents with acute haemorrhagic diarrhoea, vomiting, lethargy and leukopenia. What is the highest-priority first action?
o: Start oral metronidazole and reassess in 48 hours on the general ward.
Isolate the puppy immediately and run a faecal parvovirus antigen test, treating as parvovirus until proven otherwise.
Run a faecal flotation and defer isolation until the result is available.
e: An unvaccinated puppy with these signs is parvovirus until proven otherwise. Immediate isolation is the first step, because delay exposes susceptible animals.

q: A recently vaccinated dog tests positive on a faecal parvovirus antigen test 3 days after an MLV DAPP vaccine. How should the result be interpreted?
o: As a definitive diagnosis, so the dog is isolated and treated for parvovirus
As a probable vaccine-induced false positive, needing clinical signs and complete blood count, and PCR if ambiguous, to distinguish true infection
As proof of vaccine failure, so the dog is revaccinated with a different product
e: MLV vaccine virus is shed in faeces for up to 5 days and occasionally 2 weeks, causing false-positive antigen tests. Clinical severity and leukopenia, and PCR when ambiguous, are needed.

q: During a diarrhoea cluster in 5 dogs in one intake ward, which disinfectant is appropriate for both Salmonella and parvovirus contamination?
o: Quaternary ammonium at label dilution with 10 minutes of contact time
Bleach at 1:100 with 1 minute of contact time
Accelerated hydrogen peroxide 1:32 with at least 10 minutes of contact time
e: AHP 1:32 with at least 10 minutes of contact is effective against both. Quaternary ammonium fails against parvovirus, bleach at 1:100 is too dilute, and alcohol does not reliably kill non-enveloped viruses.

q: Which cause of feline diarrhoea needs 6% hydrogen peroxide or steam cleaning because standard bleach dilutions fail?
o: Giardia
Tritrichomonas foetus
Cryptosporidium
e: Cryptosporidium oocysts resist chlorine, including standard bleach dilutions. Steam (140°F / 60°C or above) or 6% hydrogen peroxide (30 minutes) is required.

q: A long-term cat ward has an abrupt spike in upper respiratory disease during a winter intake surge. Sanitation is unchanged, no new pathogen has entered, but major construction has begun next door. What is the most likely primary driver?
o: A new strain of calicivirus introduced by a construction worker
Failure of the ventilation system, allowing airborne spread between rooms
Environmental stress from noise and unpredictability causing immunosuppression and recrudescence of latent carriers such as herpesvirus
e: Stress is a host factor in the epidemiological triad. Noise and unpredictability immunosuppress resident cats and reactivate latent herpesvirus, so an outbreak can occur with no new pathogen and identical sanitation.

q: Thirty cats from a hoarding case arrive, and 80% have severe painful chronic stomatitis with suspected calicivirus carriage. Before committing to long-term on-site treatment, what are the most critical questions?
o: Whether the cats are pedigreed, how much they cost to house and whether a donor will pay
Whether the stomatitis is contagious to staff and how quickly the cats can be adopted
Welfare during prolonged treatment, likelihood of recovery, and whether resources allow treatment without compromising basic care for the rest of the population
e: Capacity for care is dynamic. If treating the infected group drops baseline care of the general population below minimum standards, capacity for care is exceeded.

q: An intake room is contaminated with feline calicivirus and feline panleukopenia virus. A technician proposes a quaternary ammonium product because it is cheap and pleasant smelling. What should you do?
o: Agree, provided the contact time is extended to 30 minutes.
Decline, and use an oxidising disinfectant such as accelerated hydrogen peroxide or 1:32 bleach.
Agree, provided that it is used together with 70% alcohol wipes.
e: Non-enveloped viruses lack a lipid envelope and resist quaternary ammonium and alcohol. Effective decontamination requires an oxidising agent.

q: A panleukopenia epidemic curve shows a large sharp peak on day 1 with gradual decline, then from day 8 a series of successively higher peaks about 3 to 4 days apart. How should this be interpreted?
o: It began as a point-source exposure and became a propagated animal-to-animal outbreak because isolation or sanitation failed.
It is a continuous common-source outbreak from contaminated food, with no animal-to-animal spread.
It is a normal seasonal pattern that requires no change in management.
e: A point-source spike followed by incubation-spaced peaks signals transition to a propagated outbreak, meaning isolation or sanitation has broken down.

q: During a distemper outbreak, an asymptomatic 6-month-old dog housed with a shedding puppy has a strongly positive point-of-care distemper antibody titre. What is the best management?
o: Categorise as low risk and move toward adoption without mandatory quarantine, because a positive titre over 5 months correlates strongly with protection.
Quarantine for 14 days, because positive titres over 5 months are usually false positives.
Euthanise under depopulation guidelines, because it shared housing with a shedding dog.
e: In asymptomatic animals over 5 months, a positive titre correlates with near-sterilising protection. Maternal antibody skew is the concern only in animals under 5 months.

q: During concurrent Streptococcus zooepidemicus and calicivirus outbreaks, the supervisor orders accelerated hydrogen peroxide mixed at triple the label concentration. Why should you intervene?
o: Triple concentration inactivates the disinfectant, so it is less effective than the label dilution.
Stronger-than-label disinfectant is not more effective and its caustic residues irritate the respiratory tract, increasing susceptibility.
Triple concentration is unnecessary only because the label contact time is already 1 minute.
e: Over-concentrating disinfectant adds no benefit and leaves caustic residues that damage respiratory and ocular mucosa and paw pads, raising susceptibility and mimicking a respiratory outbreak.

q: A county shelter that is legally obliged to accept strays has a virulent systemic calicivirus outbreak with 50% mortality, exhausted isolation capacity and maximum staff hours. The director demands total depopulation of all cats. According to ASV standards, what is the best response?
o: Agree, because a 50% mortality outbreak justifies euthanising all cats to protect staff.
Agree, but only after vaccinating all cats to reduce viral shedding.
Decline depopulation as the first response; stratify cohorts, create a clean break, use titres where appropriate, and work with counsel to restrict or divert intake.
e: Depopulation is a last resort. The alternative is cohort risk stratification, a clean break and titre triage, and, given a legal intake mandate, working with administrators and counsel to restrict or divert intake.

q: A veterinarian uses an FDA-approved human antibiotic extra-label for deep pyoderma in 45 confiscated dogs because no veterinary alternative exists. Which statement about records and labelling is correct?
o: No records are needed, because extra-label use is legal whenever a veterinarian prescribes it.
Records are needed for 30 days only, and only for controlled substances.
Extra-label use records (condition, species, dose, duration, number of animals) must be kept for at least 2 years and be available to the FDA.
e: AMDUCA requires a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship, records of extra-label use kept for at least 2 years and available to the FDA, and proper labelling. Laypeople cannot initiate extra-label use.

q: A technician asks to give the full daily dose of an oral beta-lactam as a single large dose once daily to save handling. What should you do?
o: Decline, because beta-lactams are time dependent and consolidating doses lets drug levels fall below the MIC.
Agree, because a higher peak concentration kills bacteria faster.
Agree, provided that the dose is given with food to improve absorption.
e: Beta-lactams are time dependent: unbound drug must stay above the MIC for about 40 to 50% of the interval. A single large dose fails, whereas high-peak killing is the aminoglycoside pattern.

q: A director wants to replace an FDA-approved ophthalmic ointment with a paste mixed by a volunteer from bulk raw drug powders bought online. What is the primary hazard?
o: The paste will be more concentrated than the approved product, so it always works faster.
Bulk-compounded products bypass manufacturing standards, risking improper potency that prolongs suffering and raises total costs.
The paste will be free of preservatives, so it is always safer for the eye.
e: Compounding from bulk raw ingredients bypasses FDA manufacturing and potency standards. Poor potency causes treatment failure and more suffering, ultimately driving costs up.

q: An isolate's MIC is well below the fluoroquinolone breakpoint, yet dogs with haemorrhagic pneumonia fail to improve on correctly dosed treatment. What is the most logical explanation?
o: The laboratory made an error, so the MIC must be repeated before any conclusion.
The drug fails to penetrate consolidated lung, or is inactivated in the purulent microenvironment of the lesions.
The dogs need a higher dose than the label because the MIC is only an estimate.
e: Susceptible in vitro can still fail in vivo, because of poor penetration of consolidated lung or sanctuary sites and inactivation in purulent, low-oxygen, acidic foci.
